terms.meaning: the lines of the innermost statements, with blank lines removed
a call to a block that strong already started but did not finish
a name written by itself in the code, like merge, with no dot in front of it
a group of blocks that reach each other through calls, directly or through other blocks
the block of the top-level code, the one whose node is None

map.name: script
map.takes: the module at import or at run
map.gives: the module names ready and main() started when run directly
map.text: script — sets up the imports, the prompt text sent to Claude, the call counter, and starts main() when the file runs as a program

children.text:
Tools this file needs:

ast — reads python source into a tree, so the file can find statements, functions and names
json — reads Claude's answer and writes map.json
re — text patterns
subprocess — starts the claude command as a child process
sys — the command line arguments and the exit on failure
Path — the file paths

jedi — finds where a name is defined and where the file uses it, for the links() rows

PROMPT = the full instruction text sent to Claude for one block

It holds the slots {name}, {code}, {block}, {span}, {ctx}, {cells}, {n} and {stmts} that compile_block() fills, all the beat, root and story rules the answer must obey, a gold example and a negative gold, and the shape of the JSON object to return.

CALLS = a one-item list that counts the calls to the claude command

A list, not a plain number, so ask_claude() can add to it from inside a function without a global statement, and main() can print the total at the end.
When a person runs this file as a program, start main(); when another file imports it, do nothing and only give the names above.

map.name: statements
map.takes: a file path and its source text
map.gives: one row per statement: nesting depth, first line, last line
map.text: statements(path, src) -> list of (depth, first line, last line) — lists every statement in a python file with how deep it is nested

children.text:
Take the file path and its source text.
When the file is not python, give back an empty list, because only python source can be parsed into statements.
rows = the collected statements, each one a depth with a first and a last line
Parse the source into a tree and let walk() fill rows, starting at depth 0 for the statements at the top of the file.
Hand back rows, the full statement list the caller uses to keep beats from cutting a statement in half.

map.name: statements.walk
map.takes: an AST node and the depth it sits at
map.gives: nothing; it fills the rows list
map.story:
Example: walk(ast.parse("if x:\n    y = 1"), 0) appends (0, 1, 2) for the if, then (1, 2, 2) for y = 1.
Only ast.stmt nodes reach rows. A child that is not a statement keeps the same depth for its own children. So depth counts statement nesting, not tree depth.
map.text: walk(node, depth) -> None — records every statement under node into rows with its nesting depth and its first and last line

children.text:
walk(node, depth) = one step down the tree from node, at the statement depth given.
It calls itself, so one call from statements covers the whole subtree.

Look at each child of node and treat it one of two ways:

A statement child: put its depth with child.lineno and child.end_lineno into rows, then walk into it with depth + 1.

Any other child, such as an expression: walk into it with the same depth, so it adds no row and no depth.

map.name: cells_of
map.takes: a file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the file's cells in file order, each with one line span
map.story:
Example: a comment on line 5 sits above a statement on lines 6-7. cells_of gives one cell 5-7, not a separate cell for the comment.
Lines that no statement owns join the span that starts after them. When no later span exists, they extend the last span. A file with no python statements falls back to runs of non-blank lines.
map.text: cells_of(path, src, lines) -> list of cells — cuts the file into the smallest pieces a beat can hold, each piece one line span

children.text:
spans = the list of line runs this function collects, one run per cell.
It starts empty, and the two paths below fill it.
For a .py file, parse the source and give each top-level statement to emit(), so spans gets one run for every smallest statement, plus the lines a parent statement holds by itself.
When spans is still empty — the file is not python — fall back to plain text: every run of non-blank lines becomes one cell, and the function returns those cells here.

covered = every line number that some span already holds.

extra = the runs of non-blank lines outside covered, such as comments, decorators, and import lines above the first statement.

Attach each extra run to the first span that starts after it: move that span's start back to the run's first line.
When no span comes after it, move the last span's end to the run's last line.
This is why every non-blank line of the file sits inside some cell.
Return the spans in file order, each one wrapped as a cell object with a single lines entry.

map.name: cells_of.kids_of
map.takes: one ast node
map.gives: the statement nodes directly below it, in order
map.story:
Example: kids_of(the for node at 76-80) gives the if node at 77-80, and nothing inside that if.
The search stops at each statement it finds. It does not stop at anything else, so a statement below an expression still comes back.
map.text: kids_of(node) -> list of ast nodes — finds the nearest statement nodes below one node, reaching down through everything that is not a statement

children.text: out = the statement nodes found so far, empty at the start

walk the direct children of node and treat each one by its kind:

a child that is a statement goes into out as it is, and the walk does not look inside it.
any other child is opened with kids_of, and the statements found under it go into out, so a statement below an expression is not lost.
give out back to the caller

map.name: cells_of.emit
map.takes: one ast statement node
map.gives: nothing; it adds line spans to spans
map.story:
Example: for an if statement on lines 85-87 with a body on 86-87, emit adds [85, 85] only.
The body lines belong to the child statements, which emit adds by their own calls.
A statement with no child statements gives its whole span, even a multi-line one.
Blank lines never start or end a span.
map.text: emit(node) -> None — walks one statement and its children, and appends to spans the line runs the node owns by itself

children.text: kids = the statement nodes directly below this node, from kids_of

A leaf statement has no child statements, so all of its lines are its own:
append the full span [node.lineno, node.end_lineno] to spans and stop here.

covered = every line number that a child statement holds.

The same loop calls emit on each child, so each child adds its own spans deeper down.

Walk the node's line numbers and collect the runs of lines that are the node's own — not in covered and not blank.
a marks the start of the open run; each break in the run appends [a, n - 1] to spans, and a run still open at the end appends up to node.end_lineno.
These runs are the header and any trailing parts of the statement, like the def line or the else line.

map.name: merge
map.takes: a list of [start, end] line ranges
map.gives: the joined ranges in line order
map.story:
Example: merge([[1, 2], [3, 3], [7, 8]]) gives [[1, 3], [7, 8]].
Ranges 1-2 and 3-3 join because 3 comes right after 2, with no gap between them. A range fully inside the range before it changes nothing, because the end keeps the larger of the two values.
map.text: merge(spans) -> list of [start, end] — sorts line ranges and joins the ones that touch or overlap into single ranges

children.text:
out = the joined ranges built so far

The input spans are sorted first, so each range arrives at or after the start of the range before it.

For each range, compare its start a with the end of the last range in out.
When a is at most that end plus 1, the two ranges touch or overlap, so the last range grows to the larger end.
When a is further away, there is a real gap, so the range goes into out as a new entry.
give back the joined ranges

map.name: ask_claude
map.takes: a prompt string
map.gives: the parsed JSON object the model returned
map.story:
Example: the model answers "Sure!\n{\"root\": {}}" and ask_claude gives back {"root": {}}.
The cut keeps everything from the first { to the last }, so words around the JSON do not break the parse.
A nonzero exit code stops the run with the last 500 characters of stderr.
The call fails after 600 seconds.
map.text: ask_claude(prompt) -> dict — sends one prompt to the claude command line tool and gives back the JSON object in its answer

children.text: count this call in CALLS, the running total of claude calls the run reports at the end

r = the finished claude command, run with the prompt and asked for JSON output

The call waits up to 600 seconds.
stop the run when claude exits with an error, and show the last 500 characters of its stderr as the reason

raw = the text of the model answer, taken from the result field of the claude output

The text can hold words around the JSON, so the return cuts from the first { to the last } and parses that part.

map.name: check_block
map.takes: the model's answer and the block's real cells, statements and essential lines
map.gives: the four checked parts of the answer
map.story:
Example: the loop at lines 181-198 can split into three beats, one for each part.
A beat that holds cell 20 and cell 21 fails, because it takes line 180 plus part of the loop.
A beat inside one statement is legal, a beat across its edge is not. The check looks only at essential lines.
map.text: check_block(m, cells, stmts, ess, label) -> root, story, terms, beats — accepts the model's answer for one block only when every field and every beat obeys the rules, and hands the four checked parts back

children.text:
check_block reads one answer m from the model and refuses it with an assert as soon as a rule breaks.

root = the root object of the answer, the one-line summary of the whole block.

The root must carry three fields, each a text that is not empty:
text — the signature line
takes — the input
gives — the output

When the block is a function, label ends with "()", and root.text must start with that same name and an open bracket.
This keeps the signature true to the code.

Read the two free parts and check their type:
story — a text, empty when the reader does not stumble
terms — a list, empty is legal

An empty story is allowed only with no terms.
Each term must be an object with a term text and a meaning text, and the term must occur word for word in the story, so no term stays unused.

beats = the list of beats, which must exist and hold at least one beat.

at = the cell number where the next beat must start, one at the beginning.

Go through the beats in order. Each one gives its cell range a to b.
The beat must start exactly at at, must end at or after a and not after the last cell, and must have text that is not empty.

got = the line numbers that the cells of this beat cover, kept down to the essential lines in ess.

This makes the beat comparable with the statements of the block.

Compare the beat with every statement of the block. The beat is good when it does not touch the statement, or holds all of the statement, or lies fully inside it.
A beat that takes only a part of a statement and also lines outside it is refused, and the message names the cells inside that statement to help the repair.
at = b + 1, so the next beat must start immediately after this one and no cell is skipped or used two times.

After the loop, at must be one past the last cell, which proves that the beats cover all cells.
Then give the root, the story, the terms and the beats back to the caller.

map.name: carve
map.takes: a line range, the ranges to remove from it, and the file lines
map.gives: the leftover line ranges, trimmed of blank lines
map.story:
Example: carve(1, 10, [[4, 6]], lines) gives [[1, 3], [7, 10]], two ranges, not one.
A removed span in the middle splits the range in two. Every returned range starts and ends on a line with text. A range that holds only blank lines drops out.
map.text: carve(a, b, minus, lines) -> list of line spans — returns the lines from a to b that no span in minus covers, with blank edges removed

children.text:
used = every line number that the minus ranges cover
These are the lines another block already owns, so this block must not claim them.

Walk the line numbers from a to b and collect each unbroken run of free lines into spans.
run holds the first line of the run in progress; a used line, or the end of the range, closes the run and appends it.
The loop goes one step past b so a run that reaches the end still closes.

Pull the blank lines off both ends of each span, then keep it only if a line with text is left.
This stops a block from starting or ending on the empty lines between definitions.
Give back the trimmed spans.

map.name: blocks_of
map.takes: a file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the blocks of the file, in file order
map.story:
Example: cells_of spans lines 71-135 and holds the nested defs kids_of and emit.
blocks_of gives cells_of only the lines 71-73 and 103-135, and makes cells_of.emit a block of its own.
The lines that no def covers become the script block. That block appears only when such lines are left.
map.text: blocks_of(path, src, lines) -> list of blocks — splits the file into one block per def or class, plus a script block for the rest, each block holding only its own lines

children.text: fns = the flat list of every def and class in the file, empty at the start

For a .py file, grab parses the source and fills fns.
Each entry holds the dotted name like cells_of.emit, the full line span, and the AST node.

A file that is not Python finds no functions, so only the script block comes out below.

blocks = one entry per def or class.

For each function f, inner collects the spans of the defs nested inside it. carve removes those spans from f, so the block keeps only the lines f writes itself and each nested def stays free for its own block.
carve over the whole file, minus the span of every def, gives the lines no function holds. These become the script block, appended only when some lines remain.
Sort the blocks by their first line and give them back in file order.

map.name: blocks_of.grab
map.takes: an AST node and the list of enclosing def names
map.gives: nothing; it fills the outer fns list
map.story:
Example: a method m inside class C gives the name "C.m", and a def inside a plain if gives just its own name.
The scope grows only for a def or class, so wrappers like if and for pass their scope through unchanged.
The span starts at the first decorator line, not at the def line.
map.text: grab(node, scope) -> None — walks the tree under one node and appends every def and class it finds to fns, with its dotted scope name and full span

children.text: grab looks at every direct child of node, one at a time

when the child is a def, an async def, or a class, record it in fns:

a = the first line of the child, counting its decorator lines, because a decorator sits above the def line and belongs to it

name = the enclosing scope names and this name joined with dots, so an inner def reads as outer.inner
span = that first line to the last line of the child
node = the AST node itself, kept for later work
grab calls itself inside that def or class, with this name added to the scope, so anything nested one level deeper gets the longer dotted name
for any other child — an if, a for, a plain statement — grab calls itself with the same scope, because only a def or a class makes a new scope

map.name: calls_of
map.takes: one block, the file's top-level nodes, and the set of all block names
map.gives: the names of the blocks this block uses, sorted
map.story:
Example: the script block holds main() at line 497, so out gets "main".
The names that main uses inside its own def never reach this list.
The loop skips top-level defs and classes, so every function keeps its own calls.
A function block scans its own node instead, and scan leaves out the defs nested in it.
map.text: calls_of(block, body, names) -> sorted list of names — lists the other blocks whose names appear in this block's own code

children.text:
Set up three names before the walk:

skip = the node types that are blocks of their own — functions, async functions and classes.
scope = the parts of this block's dotted name, empty for the script block.
out = the set that collects the names found.

Choose the nodes to walk, then let scan fill out with every block name the code under them uses.

A function block walks its own node.
The script block walks only the top-level statements that are not defs or classes, so the calls that sit inside a function stay with that function.
Give the collected names back in sorted order, so the caller always gets the same list.

map.name: calls_of.resolve
map.takes: a bare name from the code
map.gives: the matching dotted block name, or None
map.story:
Example: with scope ["cells_of", "emit"], resolve("kids_of") gives "cells_of.kids_of", not "kids_of".
The search starts at the deepest scope level and moves outward, so the nearest block wins. The last try is the bare word alone, a top-level block. No level matching means the word is a builtin, an import, or a plain variable.
map.text: resolve(word) -> full block name or None — turns a bare name used inside a block into the dotted block name it points at

children.text: Take one bare name as the caller wrote it inside the block, with no scope path on it.

hit = the current scope path cut to k levels, with the word joined on the end.

The count k runs down from the full depth of scope to zero, so the innermost enclosing name is tried first and the bare top-level name last. The first hit that is a real block name in names goes back to the caller.
Give None back when no level of the scope makes a known block name.

map.name: calls_of.scan
map.takes: one syntax tree node
map.gives: nothing; it fills the out set
map.story:
Example: in cells_of, scan adds "cells_of.emit" for the call on line 104, but reads no name inside emit itself.
A nested def or class is its own block, so scan stops at it. A bare name counts, even where the code does not call it. The block's own name never enters out, so recursion is not recorded.
map.text: scan(node) -> None — adds to out every block name that the code under node uses

children.text: scan(node) reads the direct children of one syntax tree node, one child at a time.

Pass over a child that is a function or a class definition.
skip holds those three node types. Such a child is its own block, and its names belong to that block, not to this one.

When the child is a plain name, resolve turns it into the dotted block name it points at.
Add that name to out only when it is a real block and not this block itself, so a block never lists itself.
Call scan again on the child, so the names deeper inside the same statement are reached too.

map.name: layers_of
map.takes: the blocks and the call names of each block
map.gives: one layer number per block name
map.story:
Example: carve calls nothing and blocks_of calls carve, so carve gets 1 and blocks_of gets 2.
Blocks in one call cycle all get the same number. The number counts the longest call chain below a block, not the distance down from the top.
map.text: layers_of(blocks, calls) -> dict from block name to layer number — gives every block a number that is higher than the numbers of all the blocks it calls

children.text:
Set up the record the component search in strong() writes into:

idx = the visit number given to each block name
low = the smallest visit number that block can reach
on = the block names that are still on the stack
st = the stack of block names now being visited
comp = the component key found for each block name
k = the next visit number, kept in a one-item list so strong() can change it

Call strong() once for each block that no earlier call reached.
After this loop comp holds a key for every block, and blocks that call each other in a cycle share one key.

edges = the calls from one component to another, with calls inside a component left out

A cycle is inside a single component, so what is left has no cycles and a longest chain below each component exists.

h = the height already worked out for each component

Return the height() of each block's component as that block's layer.

map.name: layers_of.strong
map.takes: a block name
map.gives: nothing; it fills idx, low, comp and empties the part of st it owns
map.story:
Example: two blocks that call each other, a and b. strong("a") sets comp["a"] = comp["b"] = "a", one group for the pair.
A block that calls nobody gets its own group: comp["a"] = "a".
The group id is the name of the block that strong reached first, not a number.
The back edge only counts when the callee is still on st, so a finished group never joins a later one.
map.text: strong(v) -> None — visits block v and its callees to find the strongly connected component that contains each block, writing every result into comp

children.text:
give v a visit number:

idx[v] = the order in which strong reached v
low[v] = the smallest idx that v can reach, and it starts at v's own idx

k[0] = the counter that gives the next visit number, so it steps by one

st = the stack of blocks with no group yet, and v joins it
on = the set of the names on st, for a fast test later

walk every block that v calls:

When the callee w is new, strong descends into it and then pulls w's low value back up into low[v].
When w is old but still on the stack, w is part of the same cycle, so low[v] drops to idx[w].
A callee that is old and off the stack belongs to a group that is closed, so this loop leaves it alone.

when low[v] is still idx[v], no call from v or below it reached higher, so v is the first block of its group.
Pop st down to v and write comp[w] = v for each block popped, which names the whole group after v.

map.name: layers_of.height
map.takes: a component key
map.gives: the height number for that component
map.story:
Example: c calls d, d calls nothing. height(d) gives 1, and height(c) gives 2.
A component with no outgoing edges gets height 1, not 0. The first call for a component fills h[c], so later calls read the stored number. The recursion is safe only because edges holds one entry per component group, so no cycles remain.
map.text: height(c) -> int — gives the longest call chain length below a component, counted through the edges map

children.text:
height(c) = the depth of the call chain under the component c.
First look in h, the store of numbers already worked out, so each component is counted one time only.

When the number is missing, take the height of every component that c calls through edges, keep the largest, and add 1 for c itself.
The default of 0 makes a component that calls nothing get the height 1.
give back the stored number for c

map.name: nodes_of
map.takes: a list of top-level tree nodes
map.gives: every node in the tree, parents before their children
map.text: nodes_of(tree) -> list of nodes — flattens the whole tree into one list of every node it holds

children.text:
out = the flat list of every node found

The caller wants one list to count or scan, not a shape it must walk itself.
walk() adds every node in the tree, and every node under them, into out, then nodes_of hands that list back.

map.name: nodes_of.walk
map.takes: a list of tree nodes
map.gives: nothing; it fills the out list
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — appends every node in a list of tree nodes, and every node under them, into out

children.text: step over each node t in the list ns and add it to out first, so a parent lands before anything under it
when the node has a children list, walk that list too, so nodes at every depth reach out

map.name: number
map.takes: the list of top-level block nodes
map.gives: nothing; it sets an id field on every node in place
map.story:
Example: two blocks, the first with one child, and that child with one child of its own.
number gives F01, F01.1, F01.2, then F02.
The child and the grandchild both sit one dot deep. The counter k counts on through every depth. number changes the nodes in place and returns nothing.
map.text: number(tree) -> None — writes an id into every node of the map: F01, F02 for the top blocks, and dotted ids under them

children.text: Take each top-level block of the tree in file order, with a count i that starts at 1.

t["id"] = the block's own id, F01 for the first block, F02 for the second.
The two digits keep the ids the same width.

k = the count of ids given out below this block, held in a list so the nested walk can raise it.

walk then numbers this block's children and every node under them, each id starting with the block's own id.

map.name: number.walk
map.takes: a list of child nodes
map.gives: nothing; it writes an id into each node it reaches
map.story:
Example: a root with id F03 and two children gives the children the ids F03.1 and F03.2.
A grandchild of the first child gets F03.3, not F03.1.1.
The counter k is one counter for the whole tree under the root, and it never resets.
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — numbers a list of child nodes and every node under them, so each one gets an id like F03.1

children.text:
walk takes a list of nodes ns and steps over each child c in turn.
It calls itself for the children of a child, so one call covers the whole tree under the starting list.

raise the counter k by one, then set c["id"] to the root id t["id"] and that count, joined with a dot.
k sits in a one-item list so the nested walk can change the same number the caller sees.
when the child holds children of its own, walk goes down into them with the same counter, so deeper nodes take the next numbers in the same run.

map.name: owner_of
map.takes: the numbered map tree
map.gives: a lookup from line number to node id
map.story:
Example: root F01 with children F01.1 over lines 1-2 and F01.2 over line 3 gives {1: "F01.1", 2: "F01.1", 3: "F01.2"}.
The root F01 owns no line, because it has children. Only a node with no children claims its lines. A line that no childless node covers stays out of owner.
map.text: owner_of(tree) -> dict from line number to node id — tells which text of the tree holds each line of the file

children.text:
owner = the lookup from one line number to the id of the node that holds it.

It starts empty and fills up line by line.

Walk every node of the tree with nodes_of, and keep only the nodes that have no children.

A node with children says nothing about single lines: its children already say it, and the deepest text is the one a reader wants for a line.
For each line range of such a node, write that node's id against every line number in the range.
Hand the finished lookup back to the caller.

map.name: links
map.takes: the source path and a map from line number to text id
map.gives: one row per shared name, with the text that defines it and the texts that use it
map.story:
Example: owner puts line 138 in F03, and a use of merge in F14.3.
links gives {"name": "merge", "def": "F03", "used": ["F14.3"]}.
The imported name ast earns no row, because goto sends it out of this file.
Uses that share the definition id are dropped, so a name used only at home gives no row.
map.text: links(path, owner) -> list of rows — finds every name that this file defines and lists which other texts use it

children.text: links takes the source path and owner, the map that says which text id holds each line.
A file that is not Python gets an empty list, because jedi reads Python only.

Set up the three things the scan needs:

p = the absolute path of the file, the value that later tells a local definition from an imported one

script = the jedi view of the file, the tool that finds names and their uses

rows = the list of finished link records

Walk every name jedi sees in the file, and drop the ones that come from somewhere else.
When goto sends a name to a different module path, the name is imported, so this file does not own it.

src = the id of the text that holds the definition line.
When no text owns that line, the name cannot be linked, so skip it.

used = the sorted ids of the texts that mention this name somewhere else in the file.
References inside the defining text itself are left out, because a link to yourself says nothing.
Keep a row only when some other text uses the name: its name, the text that defines it, and the texts that use it.
Hand back all the rows, the cross-references the reader can click.

map.name: row_of
map.takes: a cell number, the cell, and the file lines
map.gives: one text line that describes the cell
map.text: row_of(i, c, lines) -> string — writes one cell as a single prompt line: its number, its line ranges, and its first line of code

children.text:
spans = the cell's line ranges as text, like "12-14, 20-21"
A cell can hold more than one range, so join them with commas.

return the finished line: the cell number, the ranges, then the first code line of the cell, stripped of its indent.
The reader of the prompt sees where the cell is and what it starts with.

map.name: write_node
map.takes: a node dict and an indent string
map.gives: the JSON text of that node and its subtree
map.story:
The whole map is written by hand, not by json.dumps on the tree.
Each node keeps its own field order, and every field value still passes through json.dumps.
A leaf ends with "}" on its own line; a parent opens "children" and calls write_node again with two more spaces.
map.text: write_node(t, ind) -> string — turns one map node and all of its children into indented JSON text

children.text:
head = the opening text of this node, starting at the given indent with the node id.
The function builds the JSON by hand so the field order and the line breaks stay fixed.

A node with a "name" is a block root, so it gets the block fields:

name — the block name
layer — its call height
calls — the blocks it calls
takes and gives — its input and output phrases

story is added only when the block earned one.
A node with no name is a beat, so it gets only its layer.
Every node, root or beat, then gets its text and its line ranges.
A node with no children is complete: close the object and give the text back.
A node with children calls write_node on each child with two more spaces of indent, then wraps them in a "children" list and closes the object.

map.name: write_map
map.takes: an output path and the map dict with file, links, terms and map fields
map.gives: nothing; it writes the file
map.text: write_map(path, m) -> None — writes the whole map object to a file as JSON, formatted so the tree is readable

children.text:
rows = the link records, each one on its own line, joined by commas

links_part = that block wrapped in brackets, or "[]" when there are no links.
Each link stays on one line, so the file reads as a list of short records.

trows = the term records, one per line, in the same shape

terms_part = the bracketed block, or "[]" when there are no terms.
tree = the text of every root node, made by write_node with a four-space indent, one root after another.
join the file name, the links, the terms and the tree into one JSON object and write it to path.

map.name: compile_block
map.takes: one block, its cells, and the file around it
map.gives: the checked node for the block and its list of terms
map.story:
Example: a block of one cell gives a node with text, takes and gives, and no children key — its single beat text is dropped.
Every retry sends the failed answer plus every earlier error back, so the list of broken rules grows.
After 8 failed tries compile_block stops the whole program with sys.exit; it never gives a partial node.
map.text: compile_block(bl, cells, name, code, lines, stmts, ess, ctx) -> node, terms — gets one block's explanation from the model and retries until the answer passes every rule

children.text:
bstmts = the statements of the file that lie completely inside this block's lines.
The checker needs them later to test that no beat cuts a statement in half.

stext = the prompt text that lists those statements as line ranges, a child indented under its parent.
It stays empty when the block holds no statement of its own.

Fill the prompt template:

label — the block's short name with "()", or "the top-level script code" when the block is not a def
span — the block's line ranges as text
rows — one line per cell, each written by row_of
base — PROMPT with the file, the block, the cells, and ctx, the meanings of the functions this block calls

Set up the retry state:

note — the extra text put after the prompt when a try fails, empty on the first try
errs — every rule the model broke so far
m — the last answer, kept so a failed one can be shown back to the model
Try at most 8 times to get an answer that passes.
ask_claude sends the prompt and gives back the JSON object, then check_block accepts it only when every field and every beat obeys the rules and hands back root, story, terms and beats.

Build the node for this block from the accepted answer: its text, takes and gives, and all the block's lines joined by merge.
Add story only when the model wrote one, and add one child per beat only when the block has more than one cell.
Print how many cells, beats and terms this block got, then give the node and the cleaned terms back to the caller.

When the answer breaks a rule, print the reason, add it to errs, and build note: the failed answer, the rule it broke, and every rule broken before it.
The next try sends that note after the prompt, so the model repairs its own answer.
When no try passes, stop the whole program and name the block that failed.

map.name: main
map.takes: a source file path on the command line
map.gives: map.json written next to that file
map.story:
Example: cells_of sits at layer 1, main sits higher, so cells_of compiles first.
main's prompt then holds the finished line for cells_of as ctx. The tree in map.json is sorted by first line, not by this compile order. ess holds only the lines of statements that hold no other statement.
map.text: main() -> None — reads the file named on the command line, explains every block of it, and writes map.json beside it

children.text:
Read the file named on the command line and make the two views of it the prompt needs:
path = the file to explain, taken from sys.argv[1]
src = its full text
lines = its lines, without the line ends
code = the same lines with a number and a bar in front, the form the prompt shows to the model

The assert stops the run early when the file holds no code.

Get the two structures the rest of the run measures with:
cells = the smallest pieces a beat can hold, from cells_of
stmts = every statement with its depth and its line range, from statements

ess = the lines that count when a beat is checked.

Only a statement with no statement inside it puts its lines in, and blank lines come out again. An outer for line is thus not counted with its body, and check_block compares each beat against this set.

Cut the file into blocks and put them in call order:
blocks = one block per def or class, plus the script block, from blocks_of
body = the top-level nodes of the file, which calls_of needs
names = the names of the blocks that are real defs
calls = for each block, the block names it uses, from calls_of
lay = one layer number per block, from layers_of, higher than every block it calls

parts = the cells of each block, kept under the block name.
A cell goes to the one block whose line spans hold all of the cell's lines.

Three holders for the loop that follows:
done = the finished node of each block, by name
tout = the terms to write into the map
tseen = the terms taken already, so each term is written one time

Walk the blocks from the lowest layer up, so a block is explained after all the blocks it calls.

ctx = the one-line meanings of the blocks this one calls, from their finished nodes.
The prompt gets ctx so compile_block can speak of a call at its own level and not open it again.
Keep each term this block gives a meaning to, and drop a term an earlier block gave already.

Put into the node the facts the model does not supply:
name = the block name
layer = its layer number
calls = the names it calls
lines = its line spans

done then holds the node, so the blocks above it can read its takes and gives.

tree = the block nodes sorted back into file order.
number gives every node an id, and owner_of makes a lookup from line number to the id of the node that holds that line.

m = the whole map: the file name, the shared-name rows from links, the terms, and the tree.
write_map writes it to map.json in the folder of the source file.
Print the counts of the run: blocks, texts, links, terms, and calls to claude.
